note: Original plain-language summaries written for this app. Not copied from any textbook.

lessons.title: How a muscle actually contracts

sections.heading: The layers
points: Whole muscle → bundles called fascicles → single muscle fibers (cells) → myofibrils → sarcomeres.
The sarcomere is the smallest unit that contracts. Think of it as one link in a long chain.
Inside it are two protein filaments: thick ones (myosin) and thin ones (actin).

sections.heading: Sliding filament theory, step by step
points: A nerve signal reaches the fiber and causes calcium to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (the fiber's calcium storage tank).
Calcium binds to troponin, which moves tropomyosin out of the way and uncovers binding spots on actin.
Myosin heads grab actin (a cross-bridge) and pull. Breaking down ATP powers that pull (the power stroke). Then a fresh ATP has to bind so the myosin head can let go and reset.
Force at any moment depends on how many cross-bridges are attached at once.
Filaments slide past each other. They don't get shorter themselves; the sarcomere does.

sections.heading: What changes in the sarcomere
points: The I-band and H-zone shrink as the filaments overlap more.
The A-band (the length of myosin) stays the same.
When the signal stops, calcium is pumped back, and the muscle relaxes.

lessons.coach: Why it matters: fatigue in a hard set is partly the fiber struggling to handle calcium and ATP fast enough. That's one reason jump height drops late in a session.

questions.q: Which protein does calcium bind to so contraction can start?
questions.why: Calcium binds troponin. That shifts tropomyosin off actin's binding sites so myosin can attach.

questions.q: During a contraction, which part of the sarcomere stays the same length?
questions.why: The A-band is the length of the thick (myosin) filaments, and filaments don't shrink. The H-zone and I-band get smaller as overlap increases.

questions.q: What is ATP needed for in the cross-bridge cycle?
choices: Letting the myosin head detach from actin and reset
questions.why: ATP lets myosin release actin and re-cock for the next pull. No ATP means no release (that's why muscles lock up in rigor mortis).

questions.q: Where is calcium stored inside a muscle fiber?
questions.why: The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium and releases it when the fiber is stimulated.

questions.q: What is the smallest contractile unit of a muscle?
questions.why: Sarcomeres are the repeating units in a myofibril that actually shorten.

lessons.title: The three energy systems

sections.heading: The big idea
points: Muscles only run on ATP, and they only store a tiny amount. Three systems rebuild it.
All three are always on. Which one does most of the work depends mainly on intensity, and secondarily on duration.

sections.heading: The three systems
points: Phosphagen (ATP-PCr): fastest, tiny capacity. Uses creatine phosphate to rebuild ATP. Runs all-out efforts.
Glycolysis: breaks down carbohydrate (glycogen or blood glucose). Faster than aerobic, bigger capacity than phosphagen.
Oxidative (aerobic): slowest but huge capacity. Uses oxygen to burn carbs and fat. Also refills the phosphagen system during rest.

sections.heading: Duration and intensity (know this table)
points: 0-6 s, extremely high intensity: phosphagen (1RM, max jump, short sprint).
6-30 s, very high: phosphagen + fast glycolysis.
30 s to 2 min, high: fast glycolysis (a hard 400 m).
2-3 min, moderate: fast glycolysis + oxidative.
>3 min, low: oxidative.

sections.heading: Work to rest ratios
points: Training a system means matching the work to it and giving enough rest to refill it.
Phosphagen work: about 1:12 to 1:20 (5 s sprint, 60-100 s rest).
Fast glycolysis: about 1:3 to 1:5.
Fast glycolysis + oxidative: about 1:3 to 1:4.
Oxidative: about 1:1 to 1:3.
Why so much rest for phosphagen work: fully refilling creatine phosphate can take up to about 8 minutes.

lessons.coach: Why it matters: if rest is too short between sprints, you end up training glycolysis instead of top speed. Same with jump testing: rest enough so each jump is a true max.

questions.q: Which energy system mainly fuels a 1RM back squat?
questions.why: A 1RM takes a few seconds at max intensity, which is the phosphagen system's job.

questions.q: An athlete runs a hard 400 m in about 55 seconds. Which system contributes most?
questions.why: Efforts from about 30 seconds to 2 minutes lean mostly on glycolysis.

questions.q: What work to rest ratio best targets the phosphagen system?
questions.why: Phosphocreatine takes a few minutes to fully refill, so short max efforts need long rest.

questions.q: Which statement about energy systems is true?
choices: Only one system works at a time
All systems are always active; intensity mostly decides which dominates, then duration
The oxidative system shuts off during sprints
questions.why: They overlap. Intensity is the main factor in which one supplies most of the ATP, with duration second.

questions.q: Which system has the largest capacity but the slowest rate of ATP production?
questions.why: Aerobic metabolism can go for hours but can't make ATP fast enough for max efforts.

lessons.title: Sets, reps, load, and rest by goal

sections.heading: Load and reps go together
points: Load is usually written as a % of 1RM (the most you can lift once). Heavier load = fewer reps possible.
Rough guide: about 85% 1RM ≈ 6 reps, 75% ≈ 10 reps, 67% ≈ 12 reps.

sections.heading: The goal table (memorize this one)
points: Strength: ≥85% 1RM, ≤6 reps, 2-6 sets, 2-5 min rest.
Power (single-effort, like a jump or throw): 80-90% 1RM, 1-2 reps, 3-5 sets, 2-5 min rest.
Power (multiple-effort, like a basketball game): 75-85% 1RM, 3-5 reps, 3-5 sets, 2-5 min rest.
Hypertrophy (muscle size): 67-85% 1RM, 6-12 reps, 3-6 sets, 30 s to 1.5 min rest.
Muscular endurance: ≤67% 1RM, ≥12 reps, 2-3 sets, ≤30 s rest.

sections.heading: Assigning it
points: These numbers apply to core lifts (big multi-joint lifts like squats and cleans). In a strength program, assistance lifts should be no heavier than an 8RM.
Power loads look 'too light' for the reps on purpose: lighter loads let every rep stay fast, which is where peak power happens.
The 2-for-2 rule: if an athlete can do 2+ extra reps on the last set for two workouts in a row, increase the load.

lessons.coach: Why it matters: when a coach asks 'why 3x3 at 85%?' you should be able to answer with this table.

questions.q: An athlete's goal is maximal strength. Which prescription fits best?
questions.why: Strength = ≥85% 1RM, ≤6 reps, 2-5 min rest.

questions.q: What rest period fits a hypertrophy program?
questions.why: Hypertrophy uses short to moderate rest, about 30 seconds to 1.5 minutes.

questions.q: Single-effort power events (like shot put) are best trained with:
questions.why: Single-effort power uses low reps at 80-90% with full rest so every rep is fast and crisp.

questions.q: What does the 2-for-2 rule tell you?
choices: Increase load when the athlete gets 2+ extra reps on the last set two workouts in a row
Train 2 body parts twice a week
questions.why: It's a simple trigger for progressing load.

questions.q: Muscular endurance training typically uses:
questions.why: Lighter loads, high reps, short rest.

lessons.title: Motor units and fiber types

sections.heading: What a motor unit is
points: A motor unit = one motor neuron + all the muscle fibers it connects to.
When the neuron fires, all of its fibers contract fully (the all-or-none principle).
Muscles that need fine control (eye, fingers) have small motor units. Big force muscles (quads) have some huge ones.

sections.heading: Fiber types
points: Type I (slow-twitch): fatigue resistant, lots of mitochondria and capillaries, low force.
Type IIa (fast-twitch): middle ground. Fast, with more aerobic capacity and capillaries than IIx, but fatigue resistance is still only intermediate to low.
Type IIx (fast-twitch, glycolytic): highest force and speed, tires fastest.

sections.heading: How we make more force
points: Recruitment: turn on more motor units. They come on small to large (the size principle). Type I first, Type II as force needs go up.
Rate coding: fire the motor units that are already on faster.
Takeaway: to train the big fast-twitch units, you need heavy loads or fast, explosive efforts.

lessons.coach: Why it matters: light, slow sets never reach the high-threshold units that drive jump height and sprint speed.

questions.q: A motor unit is made up of:
choices: One muscle fiber and its blood supply
One motor neuron and all the fibers it innervates
All the fibers in one fascicle
questions.why: That's the definition of a motor unit.

questions.q: According to the size principle, which motor units are recruited first?
questions.why: Recruitment goes from small (Type I) to large (Type II) as force demands rise.

questions.q: Which fiber type produces the most force but fatigues fastest?
questions.why: Type IIx fibers are the fastest and strongest but have the lowest oxidative capacity.

questions.q: Increasing the firing frequency of already active motor units is called:
questions.why: Rate coding = faster firing. Recruitment = adding more units.

questions.q: Which fiber type has the most mitochondria and capillaries?
questions.why: Type I fibers are built for aerobic, long-duration work.

lessons.title: Levers, torque, and mechanical advantage

sections.heading: Torque
points: Torque = force × moment arm. The moment arm is the perpendicular distance from the joint to the line of the force.
That's why a dumbbell feels heaviest when your arm is straight out to the side: the moment arm is longest.

sections.heading: Three lever classes
points: First class: the fulcrum (joint) is between the muscle force and the resistance. Example: triceps extending the elbow against resistance (the triceps pulls on one side of the elbow, the load is on the other).
Second class: the resistance is between the fulcrum and the muscle force. Example: calf raise, rising onto the balls of your feet.
Third class: the muscle force is between the fulcrum and the resistance. Example: biceps curl. Most body joints work like this.

sections.heading: Mechanical advantage
points: Mechanical advantage = moment arm of the muscle force ÷ moment arm of the resistance.
Above 1: the muscle has an easier time. Below 1: the muscle has to produce more force than the resistance.
Most muscles work at a mechanical advantage below 1. That's why forces inside muscles and tendons are much bigger than the force on the bar or the ground.
Naming the lever class can be arbitrary in real movement. Understanding mechanical advantage matters more.

lessons.coach: Why it matters: small technique changes (bar position, torso angle) change moment arms, which changes which joints do the work in a squat.

questions.q: Torque equals:
questions.why: Torque is the rotational effect of a force: force times its perpendicular distance from the axis.

questions.q: A biceps curl at the elbow is which type of lever?
questions.why: The biceps pulls between the elbow (fulcrum) and the weight in the hand (resistance).

questions.q: Standing calf raises are the classic example of which lever?
questions.why: The ball of the foot is the fulcrum, body weight is in the middle, and the calf pulls at the heel.

questions.q: A mechanical advantage less than 1 means:
choices: The muscle force must be larger than the resistance
The muscle force can be smaller than the resistance
The joint is a second-class lever
questions.why: With a shorter moment arm than the resistance, the muscle has to pull harder than the load.

questions.q: Holding a dumbbell in a lateral raise, when is the torque at the shoulder greatest?
questions.why: The moment arm (horizontal distance from shoulder to weight) is longest when the arm is horizontal.

lessons.title: Choosing and ordering tests

sections.heading: What makes a good test
points: Validity: it measures what it claims to measure. A vertical jump is a valid test of lower body power.
Reliability: it gives consistent results. Same athlete, same conditions, similar score.
A test can be reliable but not valid. It can't be valid if it isn't reliable.

sections.heading: Test order (the exam loves this)
points: 1. Non-fatiguing tests: height, weight, flexibility, skinfolds, vertical jump.
2. Agility tests (like the T-test or pro agility).
3. Max power and strength tests (like a 1RM).
4. Sprint tests.
5. Local muscular endurance (like push-ups).
6. Fatiguing anaerobic capacity tests (like a 300 yd shuttle).
7. Aerobic capacity tests (like a 1.5 mile run or Yo-Yo test).

sections.heading: Keeping it fair
points: Same warm-up, same instructions, same time of day, same surface each time.
Between attempts: at least 2 minutes when not near max, 3 minutes when near max. Between tests in a battery: at least 5 minutes.
Recovery after a max phosphagen test takes 3-5 minutes. After a max glycolytic test, at least 1 hour.
Account for heat, humidity, and altitude.

lessons.coach: Why it matters: this is the backbone of Project 1. A jump test is only useful for flagging fatigue if it's reliable, so you know a drop is real and not noise.

questions.q: A test that gives consistent results across repeated trials is:
questions.why: Reliability = consistency. Validity = measuring the right thing.

questions.q: Which test should come FIRST in a testing session?
questions.why: Non-fatiguing tests like height, weight, and vertical jump go first.

questions.q: Which test should come LAST?
questions.why: Aerobic capacity tests are the last step in the recommended order.

questions.q: Correct order: 1RM bench, T-test, 300 yd shuttle, skinfolds
questions.why: Non-fatiguing → agility → max strength → fatiguing anaerobic.

questions.q: Which statement is true?
choices: A valid test must be reliable
A reliable test must be valid
Validity and reliability are the same thing
Reliability only matters for aerobic tests
questions.why: If results bounce around randomly, the test can't be measuring the right thing accurately.

lessons.title: Hormones and resistance training

sections.heading: Anabolic vs catabolic
points: Anabolic hormones help build tissue: testosterone, growth hormone (GH), insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1), insulin.
Catabolic hormones break tissue down for energy: cortisol is the main one.
Hormones only work by binding to receptors on cells. More hormone matters less if receptors aren't interested.

sections.heading: What workouts spike them
points: Testosterone rises acutely with big multi-joint lifts (deadlift, clean, squat), heavy loads (85-95% 1RM), moderate-high volume (multiple sets or exercises), short rest (30-60 s), and 2+ years of lifting experience.
GH rises most with high volume, moderate-heavy loads (like 10RM), and short rest (about 1 min). Higher lactate and lower pH are linked to bigger GH responses.
Cortisol also rises with high volume and short rest. Short term that's normal; chronically high cortisol can signal overtraining.

sections.heading: Sex and age differences
points: Women have much lower testosterone than men but actually higher resting GH. Their androgen receptors also respond quickly to training.
Testosterone response to training is lower before puberty and tends to decline with age.

lessons.coach: Why it matters: high-volume, short-rest work is hormonally 'loud' but also stressful. That's why it needs to be balanced with recovery.

questions.q: Which hormone is primarily catabolic?
questions.why: Cortisol breaks down tissue to free up energy. The others are anabolic.

questions.q: Which workout is MOST likely to produce a large acute growth hormone response?
choices: 1 set of 3 reps at 90%, 5 min rest
Single max jumps with full rest
questions.why: GH responds most to high volume, moderate-heavy loads, and short rest.

questions.q: Hormones affect cells by:
questions.why: A hormone only acts on cells that have a receptor for it.

questions.q: Which factor tends to INCREASE the acute testosterone response to a workout?
choices: Large muscle mass exercises like squats
questions.why: Big multi-joint lifts with heavy loads and enough volume drive the largest testosterone responses.

questions.q: Chronically high cortisol in an athlete can be a sign of:
questions.why: Short spikes are normal, but staying elevated suggests the athlete isn't recovering.

lessons.title: Macronutrients and calories

sections.heading: Calories per gram
points: Carbohydrate: 4 kcal per gram.
Protein: 4 kcal per gram.
Fat: 9 kcal per gram.
Alcohol: 7 kcal per gram (not a nutrient, but shows up on the exam).

sections.heading: Protein
points: RDA for adults: 0.8 g per kg body weight per day. General fitness: about 0.8-1.0 g/kg.
Endurance athletes: about 1.0-1.6 g/kg. Strength athletes (and mixed strength + endurance/sprint athletes): about 1.4-1.7 g/kg.
Eating protein soon after training helps, since muscle is extra sensitive to amino acids after exercise.
Amino acids build tissue. Essential amino acids must come from food. Leucine is a key trigger for muscle protein synthesis.

sections.heading: Carbs and fat
points: Carbs are the main fuel for moderate to high intensity exercise. They're stored as glycogen in muscle and liver.
Endurance and high-volume athletes need the most carbs. Needs go up with training volume.
Fat is the main fuel at rest and low intensity. Needed for hormones and absorbing vitamins A, D, E, K.

lessons.coach: Why it matters: when jump numbers dip across a heavy training block, under-fueling (especially low carbs) is one of the first things to ask about.

questions.q: How many kcal are in 1 gram of fat?
questions.why: Fat = 9, carbs and protein = 4, alcohol = 7.

questions.q: A 100 kg athlete eats 300 g of carbohydrate. How many kcal is that?
questions.why: 300 g × 4 kcal/g = 1,200 kcal.

questions.q: What is the general protein recommendation for the average (non-athlete) adult?
questions.why: About 0.8 g/kg/day. Athletes generally need more.

questions.q: Which of these is fat-soluble?
questions.why: A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble. B vitamins and C are water-soluble.

questions.q: Carbohydrate is stored in the body mainly as:
questions.why: Glycogen in muscle and liver. Triglycerides are stored fat.

lessons.title: Warm-ups, stretching, and PNF

sections.heading: Warm-up structure
points: General warm-up: about 5 minutes of slow aerobic activity (jog, skip, bike) to raise heart rate, blood flow, and muscle temperature.
Specific warm-up: movements similar to the sport, plus rehearsing the skill.
Whole warm-up: usually 10-20 minutes, ending no more than 15 minutes before the main activity.
RAMP: Raise (temperature and skill), Activate and Mobilize (dynamic movement patterns like squats and lunges), Potentiate (build intensity up to what the session needs).

sections.heading: Static vs dynamic stretching
points: Static stretch: slow, end position held 15-30 seconds. Doesn't trigger the stretch reflex, so low injury risk.
Static stretching before performance is debated. Holds over about 60 seconds are more likely to hurt power. Shorter holds (under ~45 s) have a smaller effect.
Dynamic stretching (walking knee lifts, lunges) moves through sport-like range under control. It's the preferred warm-up choice for most sports.
Ballistic stretching (bouncing) triggers the stretch reflex and needs care, especially after a past injury.

sections.heading: The reflexes and PNF
points: Muscle spindles sense stretch and trigger the stretch reflex (the muscle contracts to resist a fast stretch).
Golgi tendon organs sense tension and cause the muscle to relax. That's autogenic inhibition.
Reciprocal inhibition: contracting one muscle (like the quads) relaxes its opposite (the hamstrings).
PNF stretching (usually with a partner) uses these. Three types: hold-relax, contract-relax, and hold-relax with agonist contraction.
Each starts with a 10 s passive prestretch. Hold-relax: 6 s isometric hold, then a 30 s passive stretch. Hold-relax with agonist contraction adds reciprocal inhibition on top of autogenic inhibition.

lessons.coach: Why it matters: a standard warm-up before jump testing keeps scores comparable day to day.

questions.q: Which is best right before a speed and power session?
questions.why: Dynamic stretching keeps temperature up and rehearses sport movements. Long static holds (over ~60 s) are more likely to reduce power.

questions.q: The Golgi tendon organ causes the muscle to relax when tension is high. This is called:
questions.why: Autogenic = the muscle inhibits itself through its own GTO.

questions.q: Contracting the quads to help the hamstrings relax is an example of:
questions.why: Contracting the agonist relaxes the antagonist.

questions.q: Which structure detects stretch and triggers the stretch reflex?
questions.why: Muscle spindles sense changes in length and speed of stretch.

questions.q: A good general warm-up lasts about:
questions.why: About 5 minutes of light activity, then a sport-specific dynamic section.

lessons.title: How the body adapts to lifting and sprinting

sections.heading: Neural first
points: In the first several weeks of training, strength goes up faster than muscle size. That early gain is mostly neural.
Neural changes: more motor units recruited, faster firing, better timing between muscles, and less co-contraction from the opposing muscle.

sections.heading: Then muscle
points: Hypertrophy (bigger fibers) takes longer: usually more than 16 workouts before muscle size changes clearly show up.
Fibers grow mainly by adding more myofibrils (more actin and myosin), especially Type II fibers.
Fiber type shift: training moves Type IIx fibers toward Type IIa. Fully switching Type II to Type I (or back) is not well supported.

sections.heading: Other adaptations
points: Bone gets denser in response to loading. Bone adapts slower than muscle, often 6 months or more.
Tendons and ligaments get stiffer and stronger.
Overreaching (short-term performance dip that recovers) is fine. Overtraining (long-term decline) is the problem.

lessons.coach: Why it matters: a freshman's fast strength jump in month one is mostly their nervous system learning, so don't expect size changes to match.

questions.q: Strength gains in the first few weeks of a new program are mainly due to:
questions.why: Early strength comes mostly from the nervous system getting better at using muscle.

questions.q: Resistance training typically shifts muscle fibers from:
questions.why: IIx fibers take on more IIa traits with training.

questions.q: Muscle fiber hypertrophy mainly happens by:
questions.why: More actin and myosin are added, so each fiber gets bigger.

questions.q: A short-term drop in performance that recovers after a few days of rest is called:
questions.why: Overreaching is short-term and can be planned. Overtraining lasts weeks to months.

questions.q: Compared with muscle, bone adapts to training:
questions.why: Bone remodeling is slow, often taking 6 months or more to show changes.
